desc:
Each element of cuboids is a triple [a, b, c] of side lengths of a solid box. You may choose any subset of the boxes and stack them in a tower, rotating each box freely: any of its three sides may be used as the vertical side (its height) and the other two as width and depth.

Box X may be placed directly on box Y only if, in the orientations you picked, width(X) ≤ width(Y), depth(X) ≤ depth(Y) and height(X) ≤ height(Y). Return the greatest possible total height of a tower. A tower of a single box is allowed. For cuboids = [[50, 45, 20], [95, 37, 53], [45, 23, 12]] the answer is 190 (stack all three boxes; standing each on its longest side gives heights 45 + 50 + 95).
hints: A box has only 6 orientations, but you can avoid trying them all. If a box fits on another one in some orientation, what does that say about their sorted side lengths?

Sort the three sides of every box: x ≤ y ≤ z. Then box X can go on box Y (in some orientations) exactly when the sorted sides of X are component-wise at most those of Y. So fix each box to its sorted orientation and always stand it on its longest side z.

Sort all boxes lexicographically by their sorted sides. Now a box can only sit on boxes earlier in the list: dp[i] = z_i + max dp[j] over j < i with x_j ≤ x_i, y_j ≤ y_i, z_j ≤ z_i. The answer is the maximum dp[i].
editorial: If box X fits on box Y with some orientations, then sorting the sides of both keeps the component-wise comparison valid (the k-th smallest side of X is at most the k-th smallest side of Y, because a coordinate-wise dominance of one permutation over another implies dominance of the sorted versions). So the orientation question disappears: store every box with sorted sides (x, y, z).

A box's height contribution is maximised by using the largest side as the vertical one, and standing it that way never blocks anything: the placement rule is symmetric in the sides, so the chosen orientation only affects the height we gain. Hence we use the sorted orientation for every box in the tower and add the largest side z.

Now the boxes form a partial order (component-wise ≤). Sorting lexicographically by (x, y, z) guarantees that any box that can sit on box i appears before it. Then it is a longest-chain DP with weights: dp[i] = z_i + max(dp[j]) over earlier j that fit under the constraint. The answer is the largest dp[i]. This is O(n2) time and O(n) space, and it is the weighted analogue of the nested envelopes problem in three dimensions.
